title: Yesterday I went
goal: Talk about what has happened, and see why Mongolian has three past forms where English mostly gets by with one.
bekal: tell today's events with *-лаа* and older events with *-сан*
tell the three past forms apart and choose the natural one

dialogs.title: Яриа — Амралтын өдөр юу хийсэн бэ?

notes: ⚠️ **Mongolian has three past forms.** That sounds scary, but the difference is a lot like the difference between "just now," "yesterday," and "long ago" in English; Mongolian simply puts it **in the verb** instead of in an adverb.

**-лаа / -лээ / -лоо / -лөө = just now, today, still felt.** *Бослоо* (I've just got up), *хоцорлоо* (I've just been late). This form carries the tone "and the result is still here now," much like the English present perfect.
**-сан / -сэн / -сон / -сөн = done, yesterday, earlier, neutral.** *Боссон* (got up), *үзсэн* (saw). This is the safest form and the one most used for telling stories. **When in doubt, use -сан.**

**-в = the formal, written form.** *Боллов*, *ирэв*. You'll see it in newspapers, books, and announcements, but you'll almost never hear it in conversation. Just recognize it; you don't need to use it at A1.

⚠️ **The past is negated with -сангүй, not plain -гүй.** *Гарсан* (went out) → *гарсан**гүй*** (didn't go out). Notice that the past suffix stays and *-гүй* attaches after it. This differs from the present, which uses *-хгүй*: *гарахгүй* (won't go out).

grammars.title: Three past forms, and how to choose
body: This table is the heart of the unit. Read the "Feel" column first: that's where the difference lies, not in the spelling of the suffix.

head: Suffix
Example (*явах*)
Feel
English equivalent
rows: just now, today, result still felt
so it turns out, I've just learned, folk tales

after: **The practical rule fits in two lines.** For something that **just happened today**: *-лаа*. For everything else: *-сан*. With those two forms you can tell anything at A1 without ever sounding odd.

⚠️ A fourth form, *-жээ*, is worth recognizing even though you'll rarely use it yourself: it means "it turns out" and is used for things you've **just found out** or for stories you didn't witness. All Mongolian folk tales and legends are told in this form, so it's the signature sound of storytelling, like "once upon a time…" in English.

grammars.title: Forming and negating the past
body: From the dictionary form, drop *-х*, then add the suffix following vowel harmony. To negate, add *-гүй* **after** the past suffix.
after: ⚠️ Look at the eighth row: *өгөх* → *өглөө*, which looks exactly like the word *өглөө* (morning). Mongolian has a few pairs like this, and context always separates them, just like "bank" (money) and "bank" (river) in English.

**There's a second negative form you'll hear more often in conversation: *-аагүй / -ээгүй / -оогүй / -өөгүй*.** *Яваагүй* = hasn't gone yet; *идээгүй* = hasn't eaten yet. The difference from *-сангүй* is subtle: *-сангүй* means "didn't," *-аагүй* means "not yet." For A1, *-сангүй* is enough, but recognize the other one, because you'll hear it often.

Say it
English

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice *юу ч хийсэнгүй*, "didn't do anything." Mongolian uses **question word + ч + negative** to say "nothing," "nobody," "nowhere": *хэн ч байхгүй* (there's nobody), *хаана ч яваагүй* (didn't go anywhere), *хэзээ ч үгүй* (never). It works like English "any-": "not … anything," "not … anywhere."

blocks.title: Four words that link a story
items: *тэгээд* (teh-GĒD) — and then, so. ⚠️ This is the one used most in conversation.
*учир нь* (u-CHIR n') — because, the reason is.

head: Question
Meaning
Sample answer
rows: Did you have a good rest?

blocks.text: The last row is a question you'll hear every Monday morning in Mongolia, as often as "how are you" on other days. A natural answer isn't just "yes" but one extra sentence about what you did, just as you'd answer "How was your weekend?" in English with a short story, not a single word.

blocks.text: ⚠️ One warning that saves many visitors: **Mongolian tea comes with salt, not sugar.** *Сүүтэй цай* is tea, milk, salt, and sometimes a little fat. If you ask for *цай*, that's what you'll get. For sweet tea, ask for *хар цай* (black tea) and add sugar yourself.
